sources.claim: In fake check scams, someone sends a check for more than is owed and asks for money back; banks must make deposited funds available quickly, but it can take weeks to learn a check is fake, and the depositor owes the bank the money. A bank saying funds are available or a check "cleared" does not mean it is good.

sections.skill: Recognize payment scams and verify before paying

questions.prompt: An email from "your supplier" says their bank account changed. What should you do?

choices.text: Call the supplier at a number you already know
Reply to the same email asking if it is real
Pay the new account right away to avoid late fees
Call the phone number listed in that email

questions.correct_answer: Call the supplier at a number you already know
questions.intro: Small businesses are common targets for payment scams. FAKE INVOICES bill for things you never ordered, such as directory listings. CHANGED BANK DETAILS scams send an email that looks like a real supplier asking you to pay a new account. OVERPAYMENT scams send too much money (often by a check that later bounces) and ask you to send back the difference. Protection: match invoices to orders, confirm any bank-detail change by calling a known number (not one in the email), and never send back an "overpayment." A bank may make check funds available within days, yet the check can still be returned as fake weeks later, and the depositor owes the money.

questions.intro: Imagine someone in a uniform knocks and says, "I'm from the water company; pay me the bill in cash today." The uniform looks real, but you would call the water company at the number on your last bill before handing over money. Payment scams work the same way: an email or invoice can look official.
